segments.text: A civilian Boeing 747 freighter can lift more than 100 tons of cargo across an ocean,
and a modern main battle tank weighs around 60 tons.
Yet if you tried to drive that 60-ton tank into a standard commercial airliner without special bridging,
the tank would crush the floor beams before it reached the middle of the cabin.
Even if the floor held, you could never get the tank inside at a battlefield airstrip in the first place
because the cargo deck of a civilian wide-body jet sits 5 meters up in the air
and waits for a hydraulic scissor lift truck that only exists at peaceful international airports.
That mismatch explains why every serious air force refuses to rely on painted airliners
and builds a completely different breed of machine instead.
Here is the question this video answers.
Why does every military transport aircraft on Earth share the exact same awkward silhouette,
with wings bolted to the roof, a fat belly scraping the concrete, and an upswept tail,
even though that shape burns more fuel and flies slower than an airliner?
The answer is that a military airlifter is not designed around the hours it spends cruising in the sky.
Every part of its body is shaped around the 20 minutes it spends on a broken runway with engines running,
trying to swallow or spit out an army before someone shoots at it.
Start with the wing and the tail,
the two features that make a military transport recognizable from kimulators away.
Passenger jets mount their wings under the belly so the main landing gear can tuck neatly into the wing roots,
and the cabin stays quiet.
A military transport such as the C-130 Hercules,
the C-17 Globemaster,
the Airbus A400M,
or the Russian IL-76 bolts its wings straight across the top of the fuselage.
Doing that solves two ground problems at once.
First, hanging four huge jet engines or turbo propellers from a high wing lifts them several meters clear of the runway,
where they are far less likely to vacuum up loose gravel, sand, and shell fragments from an unimproved dirt strip.
Second, putting the structural wing box on the roof gets it out of the belly,
allowing the cargo floor to hang barely a meter and a half above the ground.
Combine that low belly with a tail fin lifted high into a T-shape,
and the entire rear end of the fuselage can swing open as a steel ramp that rests directly on the tarmac.
A truck driver or a tank crew does not need a crane or a loading tower.
They simply drive straight up the tail ramp into the fuselage the way a car drives onto a ferry.
Once that 60-ton vehicle rolls up the ramp,
the structure inside the cabin has to survive a kind of stress civilian freighters rarely meet.
A commercial cargo plane carries its 100 tons spread evenly across dozens of lightweight aluminum containers.
A military transport has to take 60 tons concentrated onto the two short steel footprints of a tank's tracks
or the four heavy axles of a rocket launcher.
So the floor of a heavy lifter like the C-17 or the giant C-5 Galaxy is built like a highway bridge,
ribbed with thick alloy beams and studded with heavy tie-down rings that can each hold tens of tons in a rough landing.
Built into channels along that floor are rows of steel rollers that flip over by hand.
Turn the smooth side up and you have a flat road with traction grates for wheeled and tracked vehicles.
Flip the rollers up and two loadmasters can push a line of cargo pallets down the cabin with their bare hands.
Along the walls, comfort disappears altogether.
A transport aircraft transforms from a freight train into a troop carrier
by unfolding rows of red nylon webbing seats clipped to the bare insulation blankets.
Hundreds of paratroopers sit shoulder to shoulder with their knees pressed toward a chain-down armored vehicle
in the center aisle, staring at the steel chains and quietly hoping the loadmaster did his arithmetic right.
On the even larger C-5 Galaxy, the entire nose cone, cockpit and all hinges upward like a visor
while the landing gear kneels hydraulically to lower the deck,
turning the fuselage into a tunnel where columns of trucks can drive in the tail and straight out the nose.
Every military airlifter also carries its own auxiliary gas turbine generator and heavy electric winches inside the hold,
so it can power its own hydraulics, light its own cabin, and drag dead vehicles up the ramp on a dark strip where no ground crew exists.
Look underneath that belly and you see the price of landing on dirt.
An airliner lands on smooth concrete several feet thick, so it can rest its weight on a few high-pressure tires.
A military transport has to land on thin tarmac, sun-baked clay, or matted steel planks laid over mud.
To keep from punching through the crust, aircraft like the C-17, the A-400M, and the An-124 pack 12-28 wide,
low-pressure tires into bulging pods along the sides of the fuselage,
spreading the weight across the ground like the feet of a caterpillar.
Getting down onto a short front-line strip also takes aerodynamic violence.
A commercial jet glides down a gentle three-degree slope and rolls for two cumulators to stop.
A C-17 approaching a threatened airfield can point its nose steeply downward and drop like an elevator
to spend as little time as possible inside the reach of shoulder-fired heat-seeking missiles,
while sensors on its belly watch for missile launches and banks of dispensers spit walls of decoy flares.
To keep the wings from stalling at low speed,
the exhaust from its four jet engines blows directly against huge titanium flaps lowered behind the wing,
generating lift straight out of engine blast.
The moment the wheels smash into the runway,
the pilot pops spoilers on the wings and throws all four engines into reverse thrust,
stopping a 200-ton aircraft in less than a kilometer,
and then uses that same reverse thrust to back the aircraft up
and turn around on a strip barely wider than its own wingspan.
Sometimes there is no runway at all,
or the ground is too hot to stop.
That is when the transport delivers its load without landing.
Flying slow with the rear ramp open in midair,
the crew releases a small drogue parachute out the back.
The wind catches the chute,
and the chute yanks a whole train of cargo pallets or light-armored vehicles
along the floor rollers and out into the sky in seconds.
In the most extreme version,
developed during the Cold War and called low-altitude parachute extraction,
the transport skimmed just two or three meters above a flat field,
without touching down while a gigantic parachute dragged an armored vehicle straight out the tail
to slide across the grass in a cloud of dust,
a maneuver that looked less like aviation and more like a controlled train wreck.
Because no single aircraft can be both gigantic and tiny,
Air Force's split transport fleets into two tiers.
Strategic lifters like the C-5 Galaxy and AN-124 are long-range giants
that haul outsized tanks and helicopters from factories across oceans to major rear bases.
Tactical transports like the four-propeller C-130 Hercules
take those loads from the rear hub and fly them into the short, rough strips near the fighting,
while middleweights like the C-17 and A-400M bridge both worlds.
Even then, airlift has a hilarious self-licking appetite for fuel.
Fly a fleet of transports into a remote base that has no fuel tanks of its own,
and half the cargo planes in the mission end up carrying nothing but bladder tanks of jet fuel
so the other half can fly home.
Which brings us to the mistake people make when they talk about military airlift.
Commentators often speak as if fleets of giant cargo planes
can supply a major war across a continent on their own.
My own reading is that airlift is the worst way on earth to sustain an army over months,
and the only way on earth to save one in 48 hours.
One medium cargo ship carries as much tonnage in a single voyage as hundreds of C-17 sorties,
at a tiny fraction of the fuel cost.
Transport aircraft are not the supply trucks of a war,
they are the fire engines, built to throw a brigade, a battery of air defense missiles,
or an emergency stock of shells across the world in a single night
to hold the line until the ships arrive.
So return to that 60-ton tank sitting inside a cabin that looks like a flying warehouse.
Every strange line on a military transport,
the wing on the roof, the potted wheels in the cheeks,
the bridge beam floor, the blown flaps, and the ramp in the tail,
exists to sever the link between heavy cargo and a civilized airport.
An airliner connects cities that are ready to receive it.
A military transport brings the airport with it.
